chunks: As for what ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar narrated from his brother Mūsā عليه السلام, he said:
I asked him about a man who plays with a woman and kisses her, then semen comes out from him—what is upon him?

He said: If desire comes, and it spurts forth, and he experiences slackening due to its خروج, then ghusl is obligatory upon him. But if it is only something for which he does not find any slackening nor desire, then there is no harm.

So this does not contradict what we have stated earlier, that the خروج of semen necessitates ghusl in every state. For his statement عليه السلام, “If it is only something for which he does not find any slackening nor desire, then there is no harm,” means when what came out was not semen, because what is considered far-fetched in customary experience and natural disposition is that semen should come out from a person while he finds for it neither desire nor pleasure. Rather, what is meant is when it becomes doubtful to a person and he thinks that it is semen, even though in reality it is not semen; he assesses it by the presence of desire in himself. So if he finds it, ghusl becomes obligatory upon him, and if he does not find it, he knows that what came out from him is not semen.

key_terms.اشْتَبَهَ: became doubtful or unclear to a person
key_terms.الشَّهْوَةُ: sexual desire used here as an identifying sign of semen
key_terms.الْخَارِجُ: the substance that exits the body and must be identified
key_terms.الْغُسْلُ: ritual bath required after the confirmed discharge of semen
key_terms.الْمَنِيُّ: semen whose discharge entails ritual consequences
key_terms.فَتْرَةً: slackening or bodily relaxation occurring after emission
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: there is no problem or legal consequence in this case

ai.seo_question: When does semen discharge require ghusl according to this hadith from al-Istibṣār?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the legal ruling of ghusl when fluid exits a man after intimate play and kissing. It explains that ghusl is obligatory when the emission is accompanied by desire and the bodily signs associated with semen, while doubtful discharge lacking these signs is not treated as semen.
